LESSONS.title: Opening and reading a file
LESSONS.goal: Read a file's contents with open and read
summary: open("name") opens a file
read() gives back the contents as a string
When you're done reading, close it with close()

cards.say: A file is a box of text with a name on it. You open it with open, read all the text inside with read(), and close it with close() when you're done. Here we use pretend practice files.
cards.code:
f = open("memo.txt")
text = f.read()
f.close()
print(text)

cards.say: read() gives back a string, so you can measure its length too. Open a file that doesn't exist and you get a FileNotFoundError clue. If non-English text comes out garbled on your own computer, add encoding="utf-8" to open.
cards.code:
f = open("memo.txt")
text = f.read()
f.close()
print("Memo:", text)
print(len(text))

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
f = open("memo.txt")
text = f.read()
f.close()
print(text)
items.explain: read() gives back the text inside the file as a string. So text holds “two buns”, the words written inside, not the file's name.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
f = open("notes.txt")
a = f.read()
f.close()
print(len(a))
items.explain: a is the string “tea”, which is three characters long. Text you read from a file works just like any other string.

items.q: Which clue (error) do you get when you run this code?
items.code:
f = open("grades.txt")
print(f.read())
items.explain: There's no file called grades.txt, so it's a FileNotFoundError. The name is the clue: read it as “couldn't find the file”.

items.q: Fill in the blank so the file's contents get printed.
items.code:
f = open("memo.txt")
text = f.___()
f.close()
print(text)
items.explain: The method that reads the contents is read(). close() gives nothing back, so None gets printed, and write() has no text to write, so you get a TypeError clue.

items.q: Put the lines in order to print the memo and then its length.
items.explain: First open, then read, then print using what you read. If you use text before reading, that variable doesn't exist yet.

items.task: Open memo.txt with open, read it with read(), and close it with close(). Print the contents with “Memo:” in front. Example: if the file says buy milk, print Memo: buy milk

tests.expect: Memo: hand in homework due Friday

hints: You read the text inside the file and print it along with “Memo:”. Read the order in the example again.
Think of three actions: open, read, close. The value read() gives back is a string.
Call read() on the f you opened and store the result in a variable. Then close() the file and print the text with the label in front.

f = open("memo.txt")
text = f.___()
f.close()
print("Memo:", text)
items.solution:
f = open("memo.txt")
text = f.read()
f.close()
print("Memo:", text)
items.explain: It stays right even when the file's contents change, so you really read the file. Open, read, close: a nice clean order.

items.q: What do you do when you're done with a file you opened with open?
items.explain: When you're done with a file, you close it with close(). You'll meet with, which closes it for you, in 11-3.

LESSONS.title: Reading line by line
LESSONS.goal: Read a file one line at a time with for and tidy it with strip
summary: for line in f gives you one line at a time
Each line comes with a newline \n at the end
line.strip() removes the newline

cards.say: Put a file in a for loop and it hands you one line at a time. But the newline character at the end of each line comes along too, so a plain print adds blank lines. Remove it with strip().
cards.code:
f = open("todo.txt")
for line in f:
    print(line.strip())
f.close()

cards.say: To count lines, add 1 to count every time a line comes in. You don't need to know what the line says. If the file is empty, the loop never runs, so count stays 0.
cards.code:
count = 0
f = open("todo.txt")
for line in f:
    count = count + 1
f.close()
print(count, "lines")

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
f = open("a.txt")
for line in f:
    print(line)
f.close()
items.explain: line already ends with a newline, and print adds another one, so a blank line sneaks in after each. strip() makes it go away.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
f = open("a.txt")
for line in f:
    print(len(line.strip()))
f.close()
items.explain: With the newline removed by strip(), “tea” is 3 characters and “iced tea” is 8 (the space counts). Without strip(), each would be one longer: 4 and 9.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
n = 0
f = open("a.txt")
for line in f:
    n = n + 1
f.close()
print(n)
items.explain: The file has four lines, so the for loop runs four times. Adding 1 to n four times prints 4.

items.q: Fill in the blank so each line prints with no blank lines between.
items.code:
f = open("todo.txt")
for line in f:
    print(line.___())
f.close()
items.explain: strip() removes the newline. split() makes a list, so the output looks different, and upper() only changes the letters to capitals, so the blank lines stay.

items.q: Put the lines in order to print each to-do, then Done at the end.
items.explain: Open, loop and print one line at a time, then print Done after the loop. A print with no indentation is outside the loop, so it shows up only once.

items.task: Read todo.txt one line at a time with for and count the lines in count. At the end, print “To-do: N”. Example: if there are three lines, print To-do: 3
hints: You're counting how many lines the file has. You don't need what the lines say, just how many.
for line in f runs once per line. What should you do to count each time around?
Add 1 to count inside the loop, then after the loop call f.close() and print the sentence with count in it.

count = 0
f = open("todo.txt")
for line in f:
    count = count + ___
f.close()
print(f"To-do: {count}")
items.solution:
count = 0
f = open("todo.txt")
for line in f:
    count = count + 1
f.close()
print(f"To-do: {count}")
items.explain: Adding 1 per line gave an exact count. It even works for a file whose last line has no newline and for an empty file, so you can trust this code.

items.q: Which method removes the newline at the end of a line?
items.explain: strip() removes spaces and newlines from both ends of a string. split() cuts text into pieces, and close() closes a file.

LESSONS.title: Writing to a file
LESSONS.goal: Save text to a file using with and write
summary: "w" erases and writes, "a" adds to the end
Put text in with f.write("text\n")
with closes the file for you when it's done
Loop over a list of names to open several files

cards.say: Give the mode "w" when you open a file, and it's for writing. write() puts text in, and to start a new line you add \n yourself. If you use with, the file closes on its own when the block ends.
cards.code:
with open("diary.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Sunny today\n")
with open("diary.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())

cards.say: "w" erases the old contents every time you open the file. To add to the end, use "a". Here Day 2 gets added after Day 1.
cards.code:
with open("diary.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Day 1\n")
with open("diary.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("Day 2\n")
with open("diary.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())

cards.say: Got several file names? Loop over a list of names with for and open each with open(name). A name stored in a variable opens just the same. Here we read two weekday files in turn.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
with open("t.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("A\n")
with open("t.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("B\n")
with open("t.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())
items.explain: Every time you open with "w", the file gets emptied. The second open erases A, and only B is left.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
with open("log.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("two\n")
with open("log.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())
items.explain: "a" keeps what's there and adds to the end. So “two” goes on the line after “one”.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
with open("t.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("A")
    f.write("B")
with open("t.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())
items.explain: write() doesn't start a new line on its own. Without \n, the text runs together into AB.

items.q: Fill in the mode so the old contents are erased and only bread is left.
items.code:
with open("memo.txt", ___) as f:
    f.write("bread\n")
with open("memo.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())
items.explain: "w" erases and writes fresh, so only bread is left. "a" would add after milk, and "r" is for reading, so write causes an error.

items.q: Put the lines in order to save coffee, then read it back and print it.
items.explain: First save it by writing, then open it again for reading. Swap the order and you'd try to read a file that doesn't exist yet, and get a clue.

items.q: What's the output?
options:
a.txt bread
b.txt jam
b.txt milk
items.explain: Following the list order, it opens a.txt first and prints each line, then opens b.txt. b.txt has two lines, so it prints twice.

items.q: Fill in what to loop over so it opens the two files in turn.
items.explain: The file name strings need to go in a list. With just "a.txt", the loop goes one character at a time and looks for a file called a, giving a clue. a.txt without quotes gives a clue that the name doesn't exist.

items.task: Get one to-do with input() (leave the parentheses empty). Use with and "w" to write() it to todo.txt, then open it again and print what read() gives. Example: if you enter laundry, print laundry
hints: You save the text you typed to a file, then read it back and show it. The mode matters.
Writing is "w"; for reading, leave the mode out. Using with twice keeps it tidy.
In the first with, write the text plus \n; in the second with, print what read() gives.

text = input()
with open("todo.txt", ___) as f:
    f.write(text + "\n")
with open("todo.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())
items.solution:
text = input()
with open("todo.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write(text + "\n")
with open("todo.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())
items.explain: Using "w" left only the new to-do, even when old contents were there. Splitting writing and reading into two withs makes it easy to read.

items.q: What happens when you write() to a file opened in "a" mode?
options: It adds after the existing contents
It erases the existing contents and writes
items.explain: "a" is the first letter of append. It leaves the existing contents alone and adds to the very end.

LESSONS.title: Reading a CSV table
LESSONS.goal: Read a table file with csv.reader and calculate with it
summary: CSV is a table with cells split by commas
csv.reader gives each line as a list
Cells are strings, so convert them with int()

cards.say: CSV is a table file where commas split the cells. After import csv, pass the file to csv.reader and each line comes as a list of cells. Adding newline="" when you open it is the standard rule.
cards.code:
import csv
f = open("menu.csv", newline="")
for row in csv.reader(f):
    print(row)
f.close()

cards.say: Every cell is a string, so convert it with int() to do math. Cell numbers start at 0. This CSV has no header line like “item,price”; values start on the first line, so we calculate every line.
cards.code:
import csv
f = open("menu.csv", newline="")
for row in csv.reader(f):
    print(row[0], int(row[1]) + 500)
f.close()

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
import csv
f = open("a.csv", newline="")
for row in csv.reader(f):
    print(row[1] + row[1])
f.close()
items.explain: row[1] isn't a number, it's the string "3000". + between strings sticks them together, so you get 30003000.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
import csv
f = open("a.csv", newline="")
for row in csv.reader(f):
    print(len(row))
f.close()
items.explain: Commas split it into three cells, so row is a list of length 3. len(row) tells you the number of cells.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: The only line where int(row[1]) is greater than 6 is b,7. Its name cell row[0], b, gets printed.

items.q: Fill in the blank so the amounts add up.
items.code:
import csv
total = 0
f = open("a.csv", newline="")
for row in csv.reader(f):
    total = total + ___(row[1])
f.close()
print(total)
items.explain: int() turns a string cell into an integer. str() tries to add a string to a number and gets a TypeError, and len() would add up the character counts.

items.q: Put the lines in order to split each line at commas and print only the menu names.
items.explain: This does by hand what csv.reader does. strip the line and split it at commas, and you get the same list of cells, then print row[0].

items.task: ledger.csv has no header line; each line is “item,amount”. Read it with csv.reader, add up all the amounts (convert with int), and print “Total: N won”. Example: coffee,4500 and bread,3000 give Total: 7500 won
hints: You're adding up all the amounts. What do 4500 and 3000 from the example add up to?
The amount cell is a string. Convert it with int() before adding. Numbers start at 0, so the amount is row[1].
Loop over the reader with for, turn each row[1] into an integer and add it to total, then print the sentence after the loop.

f = open("ledger.csv", newline="")
for row in csv.reader(f):
    total = total + ___(row[1])
f.close()
items.solution:
import csv
total = 0
f = open("ledger.csv", newline="")
for row in csv.reader(f):
    total = total + int(row[1])
f.close()
print(f"Total: {total} won")
items.explain: Converting cells with int() before adding makes it right no matter how many lines there are. Even the file with no lines correctly gives Total: 0 won.

items.q: What does one line from csv.reader look like?
items.explain: A line is split at the commas and comes as a list, like ["coffee", "4500"]. Every value in the cells is a string.

LESSONS.title: Chapter 11 checkpoint
LESSONS.goal: Read and write files, and read tables to sort out data
summary: open, read, close, and with
Read lines with for, tidy them with strip
"w" erases, "a" adds to the end

cards.say: Time to wrap up Chapter 11. Open, read line by line, write when you need to, and read tables with csv. We'll finish by tidying up an attendance sheet.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
f = open("memo.txt")
text = f.read()
f.close()
print(text[0])
items.explain: The text from read() is the string “bake bread”, and text[0] is its first character. Everything you know about strings still works.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
f = open("a.txt")
for line in f:
    print(line.strip()[0])
f.close()
items.explain: strip() removes the newline, then only the first character is printed. “apple” gives a and “pear” gives p, with no blank lines in between.

items.q: Fill in the mode so the new text goes after the old text.
items.code:
with open("t.txt", ___) as f:
    f.write("new\n")
with open("t.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())
items.explain: Adding to the end is "a". "w" erases the old text and leaves only “new”, and "r" is for reading, so write causes an error.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
import csv
total = 0
with open("a.csv", newline="") as f:
    for row in csv.reader(f):
        total = total + int(row[1])
print(total)
items.explain: 5 and 7, converted with int(), add up to 12. If you'd forgotten int(), adding a string to a number would have caused a TypeError.

items.q: Put the lines in order to print each number doubled, then Done at the end.
items.explain: Open, read each line and print it doubled, then print Done after the loop. int() ignores the newline at the end of the line on its own.

items.task: attend.txt has one name per line for everyone who showed up. Read it with for, count each name in the dictionary counts, and print “name: N” in the order names first appear. Example: Minsu, Jia, Minsu gives Minsu: 2 / Jia: 1
hints: You count how many times each name shows up. In the example, why is Minsu 2?
Think of a dictionary. If it's a new name, set it to 0, and add 1 every time you see it.
Read the file line by line, fill counts with the stripped name, then loop over counts with for and print.
items.explain: You finished the whole flow: sort a file into a dictionary, then print it. It works for a file with just one person and for a file with the same name several times in a row.

items.q: What happens to the file when a with open(…) as f: block ends?
items.explain: with closes the file for you when you leave the block. So it's safe even if you forget close().

ADVANCED.title: Merging files
ADVANCED.goal: Read several files and merge them into one
summary: Loop over a list of names to open the files
Open the merged file with "w" only once
Join each line with strip() + "\n"

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. You don't need it to unlock the next chapter. In 11-3 you looped over a list of names to open files, right? Write into a merged file inside that loop, and several files become one.
cards.code:
names = ["mon.txt", "tue.txt"]
with open("all.txt", "w") as out:
    for name in names:
        with open(name) as f:
            for line in f:
                out.write(line)
with open("all.txt") as f:
    print(f.read().strip())

cards.say: Open the merged file (all.txt) with "w" only once, outside the loop. Open it again inside the loop and it gets erased every time. If a file's last line has no newline, the text runs together, so add \n to every line yourself.
cards.code:
names = ["a.txt", "b.txt"]
with open("all.txt", "w") as out:
    for name in names:
        with open(name) as f:
            for line in f:
                text = line.strip()
                out.write(text + "\n")
with open("all.txt") as f:
    print(f.read().strip())

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
names = ["a.txt", "b.txt"]
with open("all.txt", "w") as out:
    for name in names:
        with open(name) as f:
            for line in f:
                text = line.strip()
                out.write(text + "\n")
with open("all.txt") as f:
    print(f.read().strip())
items.explain: Following names in order, it writes bread from a.txt, then jam and milk from b.txt. All three lines end up in all.txt, in order.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
names = ["a.txt", "b.txt"]
with open("all.txt", "w") as out:
    for name in names:
        with open(name) as f:
            for line in f:
                out.write(line)
with open("all.txt") as f:
    print(f.read().strip())
items.explain: The last line of a.txt has no newline, so line is just “x”. Write it as-is and “y” sticks right after it, making xy.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
names = ["a.txt", "b.txt"]
with open("all.txt", "w") as out:
    for name in names:
        with open(name) as f:
            for line in f:
                text = line.strip()
                out.write(text)
with open("all.txt") as f:
    print(f.read().strip())
items.explain: strip() removed the newline, and nothing put it back. write doesn't start new lines on its own, so it all runs together as breadjam.

items.q: Fill in the mode so both files are kept.
items.code:
for name in ["a.txt", "b.txt"]:
    with open("all.txt", ___) as out:
        with open(name) as f:
            out.write(f.read())
with open("all.txt") as f:
    print(f.read().strip())
items.explain: all.txt is opened again on every loop, so "a" (add to the end) is right. "w" erases it each time and leaves only jam, and "r" is for reading, so opening an all.txt that doesn't exist yet gives a clue.

items.q: Put the lines in order to count all the lines in both files and print the total.
items.explain: Start total at 0, open each file, and add 1 per line. Print just once, after all the loops are done, to get the total of 3.

items.task: Open a.txt, b.txt and c.txt in turn with for and with. Strip each line, add \n, and write it to all.txt (open all.txt only once, with with and "w"). Then read() all.txt and print it after strip(). Example: sunny, rain, cloudy, one line per file, gives three lines

tests.expect:
Mon: exercise
Tue: reading
Wed: rest

a
b
c
d
e
f

hints: You gather the lines of three files into one file, then read that file back and show it. Read the example again.
Open the merged file with "w" just once, and inside it loop over the list of names with for, opening each file.
write every line, adding the newline yourself. When you're done writing, open a new with, read(), strip, and print.
items.solution:
names = ["a.txt", "b.txt", "c.txt"]
with open("all.txt", "w") as out:
    for name in names:
        with open(name) as f:
            for line in f:
                text = line.strip()
                out.write(text + "\n")
with open("all.txt") as f:
    print(f.read().strip())
items.explain: You opened the merged file once and looped over the list of names. It works even with a mix of files that end without a newline and empty files, so you can trust this code.

items.q: When merging several files into one, how do you open the merged file?
options: With "w", only once, outside the loop
items.explain: "w" erases the contents every time it opens, so open it once and loop inside. To reopen it for every file, you'd need "a".

ADVANCED.title: Writing CSV
ADVANCED.goal: Write a table to a CSV file with csv.writer
summary: csv.writer(f) makes a writing tool
writerow([cell, cell]) writes one line
Add newline="" when writing too

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. You don't need it to unlock the next chapter. In 11-4 you read with csv.reader, right? To write, make a csv.writer(f) and pass a list of cells to writerow.
cards.code:
import csv
name = "menu.csv"
with open(name, "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["coffee", 4500])
    w.writerow(["latte", 5000])
with open(name) as f:
    print(f.read().strip())

cards.say: A list of lists works too: loop with for and write one line at a time. Numbers are saved in the file as text, so they come back as strings when you read them. newline="" is the rule that stops newlines from doubling up and adding blank lines.
cards.code:
import csv
name = "p.csv"
rows = [["tea", 4500], ["pie", 3000]]
with open(name, "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    for row in rows:
        w.writerow(row)
with open(name, newline="") as f:
    for row in csv.reader(f):
        print(row)

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
import csv
name = "t.csv"
with open(name, "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["a", 1])
with open(name) as f:
    print(f.read().strip())
items.explain: writerow joins the list's cells with commas and writes them as one line. No brackets or quotes go into the file, just a,1.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
import csv
name = "t.csv"
with open(name, "w", newline="") as f:
    csv.writer(f).writerow([1, 2])
with open(name, newline="") as f:
    for row in csv.reader(f):
        print(row[0] + row[1])
items.explain: Even the numbers 1 and 2 are saved in the file as text. row[0] and row[1] come back as strings, so adding them sticks them together: 12.

items.q: Fill in the blank to make a writing tool.
items.code:
import csv
name = "t.csv"
with open(name, "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.___(f)
    w.writerow(["bread", 2])
with open(name) as f:
    print(f.read().strip())
items.explain: The writing tool is csv.writer. csv.reader is for reading and has no writerow, and csv has no open, so both give a clue.

items.q: Fill in the method name so one line gets written.
items.code:
import csv
name = "t.csv"
with open(name, "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.___(["bread", 2000])
with open(name) as f:
    print(f.read().strip())
items.explain: The method that writes one line is writerow. This tool has neither write nor append, so those give a clue.

items.q: Put the lines in order to save a CSV, then read it back and print it.
items.explain: After import, open for writing, make a writer, and write with writerow. Once the block ends and the file is closed, open it again and read.

items.task: Read a menu item and a price with input(), one per line (leave the parentheses empty). Turn the price into int and add 500. Open order.csv with with, and use csv.writer and writerow to write one line: [name, price]. Then open it again and print what read() gives, after strip(). Example: coffee, 4500 gives coffee,5000
hints: You make one CSV line from the menu item and price you got, then read it back and show it. Read the example again.
Input is a string, so convert the price with int before adding. To write, open with "w" and newline="".
Make a writing tool with csv.writer and pass the list [name, price] to writerow. Then read it in a new with.

fn = "order.csv"
with open(fn, "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow([name, ___])
with open(fn) as f:
    print(f.read().strip())
items.solution:
import csv
name = input()
price = int(input()) + 500
fn = "order.csv"
with open(fn, "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow([name, price])
with open(fn) as f:
    print(f.read().strip())
items.explain: You wrote one line with writer and opened the file again to check. It's right for different inputs, so you really built the CSV from the input.

items.q: What's the rule when opening a file to write with csv.writer?
items.explain: Just like reading, add newline="" when writing. That way newlines don't double up and add blank lines.

cards.say: One step further: this time we combine A1 and A2 to tidy up a diary. Diary files sometimes have blank lines. If a stripped line is "", it's blank, so skip it with continue; otherwise split it at the comma.
Count inside the reading loop, then write the result with writerow to a CSV you opened once outside. Here we save each file's line count, without blank lines, as [file name, line count].
cards.code:
import csv
fn = "sum.csv"
with open(fn, "w", newline="") as g:
    w = csv.writer(g)
    for name in ["a.txt", "b.txt"]:
        n = 0
        with open(name) as f:
            for line in f:
                if line.strip() != "":
                    n = n + 1
        w.writerow([name, n])
with open(fn) as f:
    print(f.read().strip())

items.explain: A stripped blank line is "", with no characters at all. Compare with " " or "\n" and the blank line doesn't match, so all three lines get counted.

items.q: Put the lines in order to print only the moods from the diary, one per line.
items.explain: Open, split each line at the comma and print the mood cell, then close when the loop ends. close is outside the for, so it has no indentation.

items.task: may.txt and jun.txt have one “date,mood” per line, plus some blank lines. Read both with for and with, skip blank lines, split(",") the rest, and count each mood in counts. Write “mood,count” rows to mood.csv with csv.writer and writerow, in first-seen order. Then read() it and print it after strip(). Example: good, good, okay → good,2 and okay,1
hints: You count each mood across two months of diary and save the counts as CSV. Look at why good is 2 in the example.
Skip blank lines with continue, count with get(key, 0) + 1 from Chapter 8, and write each line with the writer from 11-A2.
After all the reading loops are done, open mood.csv with "w", loop over counts with for, and write [mood, count].
items.solution:
import csv
counts = {}
for name in ["may.txt", "jun.txt"]:
    with open(name) as f:
        for line in f:
            text = line.strip()
            if text == "":
                continue
            mood = text.split(",")[1]
            n = counts.get(mood, 0)
            counts[mood] = n + 1
fn = "mood.csv"
with open(fn, "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    for mood in counts:
        num = counts[mood]
        w.writerow([mood, num])
with open(fn) as f:
    print(f.read().strip())
items.explain: You linked reading, skipping blank lines, counting and writing CSV into one flow. It even handles empty files and files that end without a newline, so you can trust it.

items.q: Inside a loop, which keyword skips just a blank line and moves on to the next one?
items.explain: continue skips just this line and keeps the loop going. break ends the whole loop, so you'd miss the rest of the diary.
